::: {.guiding-q}
What is a statistical model?
:::

## In this session

- Why statistics in CBB research: description, estimation, inference, prediction
- A statistical model = a **systematic part** (what we expect) + a **random part** (how observations scatter around it)
- The linear model as the common language of this course
- From research question to model: response, predictors, unit of observation
- Course overview and workflow (R projects, Quarto, reproducibility)

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Assumptions (of the linear model)](../../glossary.qmd#assumptions), [Residuals](../../glossary.qmd#residuals)
:::

## Learning goals

After this session you can

- explain what a statistical model is and which parts it has,
- write a simple linear model as an equation and translate it into words,
- set up an R project with a Quarto document for your analyses.

## Simulate first

Before we fit anything, we write down a model and let it generate data. Here: body mass (kg) increases with age (years), plus random variation.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
set.seed(1)
n    <- 50
age  <- runif(n, 1, 10)
b0   <- 3; b1 <- 0.8; sigma <- 1.5        # the "true" model
mass <- b0 + b1 * age + rnorm(n, 0, sigma)

plot(age, mass, pch = 19, col = "#1b6f8a",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Body mass (kg)")
abline(b0, b1, col = "#c0392b", lwd = 2)   # the systematic part
```

::: {.box}
**Systematic part:** $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{age}_i$  
**Random part:** $y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$
:::
